newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul stocks falter on scepticism over law debate.
newsitem.headline: Seoul stocks falter on scepticism over law debate.

text.p: South Korean stocks are set for rocky trading on investor fears that compromise over a controversial labour law will not solve industrial unrest or help rejuvinate the economy, brokers said on Tuesday.

They said investors worried that drawn out political horse-trading would dilute benefits to industry from the new law, which was rammed through parliament on December 26, sparking more than three weeks of strikes.
President Kim Young-sam said on Tuesday the law, which makes it easier for firms to sack workers and replace strikers, would be sent back to parliament for debate.

His announcement following a meeting with opposition leaders came after the market closed, but brokers said investors had already anticipated the talks would be a setback for measures needed to help get South Korea's economy back on track.
"Kim's back-down will make union leaders heros, while inviting criticism from employers," said Lee Hahn-ku, president of the Daewoo Research Institute.
The government has said the new law would be crucial to make the labour market more flexible, thus allowing companies to trim costs and improve international competitiveness.
The composite stock index shed 27.92 points, or 3.89 percent, to finish at 690.54 on Tuesday.

"The debate on the labour issue is likely to drag on into the approaching wage negotiating season, sapping the nation's political and economic energy," said Yoo Jae-kyong of Daishin Securities. Wage negotiations usually begin around April.

Kim's climbdown on the law, which in its present form also delays recognition of the militant Korean Confederation of Trade Unions until 2000, was intended to calm industrial unrest that has caused production losses in excess of $3 billion.
The president had previously refused to discuss the law with opposition parties.
"The concession will give short-term relief to current problems, but a long-term headache to the economy," said Kim Joon-il, an economist at the state-run Korea Development Institute.
Brokers said sentiment had turned sour before President Kim's announcement.
"Investors must have found out there would be little for President Kim to offer. He was in a no-win position from the beginning," said Jeon Jeong-tak of Hyundai Securities.
A belief the market was oversold also sparked institutional selling on Tuesday, brokers said.
"The fall was anticipated after Monday's surge," said Jeon of Hyundai.
Selling pressure by institutions mounted after the index had gained about 120 points, or 20 percent, in a two-week period up to Monday, brokers said.

"There was a widespread consensus that the market was overly sold. That prompted buying, with adverse effects of the labour unrest largely ignored in this period," said Choo Hee-yup, a broker at Donwong Securities.
Rising customer deposits at brokerages and falling interest rates played a major role in the recent rally.

But customer deposits, used by securities houses to invest on the market, fell by 20 billion won ($23.5 million) over the last two days to 2.9 trillion won and yields for three-year corporate bonds rose to 12.02 percent from Monday's 11.85.
"Investors will be looking at market fundamentals now after recent hectic trading," said Jeon of Hyundai.
Brokers forecast the main index would range from 600 to 720 points for the next couple of months.
